statement: Seven different whole numbers are written around a circle. A number is called a peak if it is bigger than both of the numbers next to it. What is the smallest possible number of peaks?

choices.misconception: I thought the numbers could be placed so that none of them is a peak, but the largest number is bigger than both of its neighbours, so it is always a peak.
I thought the largest and the second largest numbers are always peaks, but the second largest can sit right next to the largest, and then it is not a peak.
I found the largest possible number of peaks, by placing big and small numbers in turn, instead of the smallest.
I counted a number as a peak when it is bigger than at least one of its neighbours instead of both, and with that rule the fewest I could get was 4.

hints: Think about the largest of the seven numbers.
The largest number is bigger than every other number, so it is bigger than both of its neighbours. That gives at least one peak. Now try to place the numbers so that no other number is a peak.
Try going up and then down round the circle, for example 1, 2, 3, 7, 6, 5, 4.

solutions.reliable: Whatever the numbers, the largest one is bigger than both of its neighbours, so there is always at least one peak. One peak is possible: write the numbers going up to the largest and then going down, such as 1, 2, 3, 7, 6, 5, 4 round the circle. Then 1 is smaller than 2, 2 is smaller than 3, 3 is smaller than 7, 6 is smaller than 7, 5 is smaller than 6 and 4 is smaller than 5, so none of them is a peak. Only 7 is a peak, so the smallest possible number of peaks is 1. The transferable idea: start with the largest (or smallest) object, because it always has the property, then build an example to show the bound can be reached.

whyOnTest: The extremal principle is tested: the largest number always has the property, which gives a lower bound, and one simple arrangement shows the bound is reached.
